title: Predict the physics: what happens when you let go?
description: A chain leaps out of a jar before it falls. A water drop lasts longer on a hotter pan. A handle spun in orbit flips over and back on its own. A ball on the longer, curvier track wins the race. Each question gives you the setup as a diagram. Read it, commit to an answer, then watch the demonstration.

questions.title: You pull one end of a long bead chain out of a jar on a high shelf and let it fall to the floor. Once the chain is flowing, what happens where it leaves the jar?
questions.description: The jar stays put. Nothing touches the chain except the jar, the air, and the floor.

images.alt: Side view of the chain fountain setup. A jar holding a loose pile of bead chain stands on a shelf. One end of the chain leaves the pile, passes through a dashed box marked with a question mark just above the jar's rim, then falls as a long dotted line to the floor. A labelled arrow marks the drop height from the shelf down to the floor.

options.text: The chain rises in a steady arc above the rim, with a clear gap between the arc and the jar
The chain drags across the rim and stays in contact with it the whole way down
The chain flows for a second and then stalls, because the pile tangles behind it
The chain leaves the rim sideways, then turns a sharp corner and drops straight down

questions.explanation:
The chain does not slide over the rim. It climbs above it and holds a steady arc there while the rest of the chain feeds through. The effect is called the chain fountain, or the Mould effect after Steve Mould, who showed it to a wide audience in 2013.

The flow is the easy part. The hanging length of chain is heavy, it pulls on the chain behind it, and that tension drags new links out of the pile, so the flow keeps itself going once it starts. The arc is the hard part. Tension can only pull along the chain, and the chain runs from the pile up to the rim and down the far side, so tension alone can never lift a link higher than the rim it is being pulled over. Something has to push the links up. John Biggins and Mark Warner showed in 2014 that a fountain is impossible without such a push, worked out how big it has to be, and measured its consequences.

The flow on its own has been a party trick for a long time, under the name Newton's beads. The arc is what turned it into a research paper.
questions.references: [Proceedings of the Royal Society A: Understanding the chain fountain](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.2013.0689) · [arXiv preprint of the same paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.4056) · [Wikipedia: Chain fountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain_fountain)

questions.title: Tension pulls along a chain, so it cannot lift a bead above the rim it is being pulled over. Where does the upward force on the beads come from?
questions.description: This is a ball chain: short rigid beads threaded on a flexible cord, so each bead behaves like a tiny rod.

images.alt: Two-panel close-up of a single chain link. Left panel: one short stiff link lies flat and at rest on top of the packed pile. Right panel: the same link a moment later, tilted. An arrow shows its upper end pulled up by the chain above while its lower end is still down against the pile, and a dashed circle with a question mark marks the contact point.

options.text: From the pile itself: as the moving chain yanks one end of a bead, the bead pivots against the pile below it, and the pile pushes back up
From air dragged along by the fast-moving chain, which lifts the arc the way moving air lifts a wing
From elastic energy stored while the chain sat coiled in the jar, released as each bead straightens out
From the rim, which acts as a pulley, and a pulley redirects tension upward

questions.explanation:
Biggins and Warner named it an anomalous reaction force from the pile. It exists because a bead chain is not perfectly limp. Each bead is a short rigid body, and each joint between beads can only bend so far. When the moving chain jerks one end of a bead upward, the bead cannot glide up. It rotates about its other end, which is still buried in the pile. That end presses down, and by Newton's third law the pile presses back up. Add that up over every bead being picked up, and the force grows with the square of the chain speed, because a faster chain picks up more beads per second and gives each one a harder kick.

A pulley can only bend the chain around the rim. It cannot hold the chain above itself. There is no elastic energy to release either, since a bead chain resting in a jar is not a wound spring. And the arc height tracks the drop height, which is what a speed-dependent reaction from the pile predicts and air does not.

Which detail of the bead geometry supplies most of the kick is still argued about, and Mould has since built rod and spool rigs to pull the mechanism apart. Every account of the fountain needs the pile to push.
questions.references: [Proceedings of the Royal Society A: Understanding the chain fountain](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.2013.0689) · [arXiv preprint of the same paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.4056) · [Wikipedia: Chain fountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain_fountain)

questions.title: You move the same jar and chain from a shelf 1 m above the floor to a shelf 2 m above it. What happens to the height of the arc above the jar?

images.alt: Side view of the chain fountain setup. A jar holding a loose pile of bead chain stands on a shelf. One end of the chain leaves the pile, passes through a dashed box marked with a question mark just above the jar's rim, then falls as a long dotted line to the floor. A labelled arrow marks the drop height from the shelf down to the floor.

options.text: It roughly doubles, because the arc height grows in proportion to the drop height
It stays the same, because the arc height is set by the size of the beads
It gets lower, because a faster chain flattens the arc out
It grows about fourfold, in proportion to the square of the drop height

questions.explanation:
A longer drop means more hanging chain, more weight pulling on the flow, and a faster chain. The reaction force from the pile grows with the square of the chain speed, and that square grows in proportion to the drop height. So the force grows in proportion to the drop height, and so does the arc it can hold up. Biggins and Warner predicted that straight-line relation from their model and then confirmed it by measurement, which is the strongest evidence that the extra force is real.

With a jar 30 m up and enough chain to feed it, the arc stands about 2 m above the rim.
questions.references: [Proceedings of the Royal Society A: Understanding the chain fountain](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.2013.0689) · [arXiv preprint of the same paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.4056) · [Wikipedia: Chain fountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain_fountain)

questions.title: You run the experiment again with a limp silk cord of the same mass per metre in place of the bead chain. What do you see?

images.alt: Side view of the chain fountain setup. A jar holding a loose pile of bead chain stands on a shelf. One end of the chain leaves the pile, passes through a dashed box marked with a question mark just above the jar's rim, then falls as a long dotted line to the floor. A labelled arrow marks the drop height from the shelf down to the floor.

options.text: The cord still flows out of the jar on its own, but it hugs the rim and forms no arc above it
An arc as high as the bead chain gave, since only the mass per metre matters
A higher arc, because a limp cord bends more easily than a chain
Nothing at all: a cord cannot pull itself out of a jar

questions.explanation:
Self-siphoning needs no stiffness. Any heavy flexible line will flow out of a jar once a falling length starts pulling on it, and a rope or a heavy cord does it readily. The arc is the part that needs the beads.

A limp cord bends freely right where it leaves the pile. Yank one end of a short section and the section simply straightens. Nothing levers against the pile, so the pile has nothing to push back against. That is why the fountain shows up with ball chain and not with string, and why the published explanation rests on the bending limit at each joint rather than on the chain's weight. If you want to try this at home, buy a long ball chain with small, closely spaced beads. It gives the cleanest arc.
questions.references: [Proceedings of the Royal Society A: Understanding the chain fountain](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.2013.0689) · [arXiv preprint of the same paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.4056) · [Wikipedia: Chain fountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain_fountain)

questions.title: A drop of water on a pan at 150 °C is gone in a second or two. You heat the same pan to 250 °C and add an identical drop. How long does this one last?
questions.description: Both figures are the temperature of the pan's surface, not of the flame under it.

images.alt: Two side-by-side panels show the same drop of water above the same pan surface, one labelled 150 degrees Celsius and one labelled 250 degrees Celsius. Each has flames beneath it and a question mark under the caption asking how long the drop lasts.

options.text: Far longer, often tens of seconds
A little less time, because a hotter pan delivers heat faster
About the same, because the drop still has to absorb the same latent heat
It flashes to steam on contact, too fast to follow

questions.explanation:
Past a threshold called the Leidenfrost point, around 193 °C for water on a smooth surface, the underside of the drop flashes to steam the instant it arrives, and the drop rides on that cushion of its own vapour. Steam conducts heat poorly next to hot steel, so a drop that has stopped touching the pan is insulated from it and survives far longer than a drop that wets a cooler surface.

The Victorian boiler engineer William Fairbairn quoted measurements of exactly this. A drop that vaporised almost at once on a surface at 168 °C lasted 152 seconds at 202 °C. He cared because the same film was wrecking heat transfer inside his boilers.

Cooks use the crossover as a thermometer. Water that hisses and spreads means the pan is hot but still wetting. Water that balls up and skates around means the surface has passed the Leidenfrost point.

questions.title: Why does the hotter pan take so much longer to boil the same drop away?

images.alt: Two side-by-side panels show the same drop of water above the same pan surface, one labelled 150 degrees Celsius and one labelled 250 degrees Celsius. Each has flames beneath it and a question mark under the caption asking how long the drop lasts.

options.text: The drop rides on a film of its own vapour, and that film carries heat far worse than direct contact with the metal
The pan radiates most of its energy away as infrared before the drop can absorb it
Water heated past 200 °C stops taking in latent heat and can only get hotter
The drop spins fast enough on the smooth pan to throw off heat as it goes

questions.explanation:
Liquid touching metal carries heat well, and that is what a drop on a 150 °C pan gets. It wets the surface, boils hard from underneath, and is gone in about a second. Above the Leidenfrost point the drop never touches at all. Vapour forms faster than it can escape sideways, so a film too thin to see holds the drop up, and heat now has to cross that film by conduction and radiation through steam.

Two things follow. The drop lasts far longer, and it slides around the pan almost without friction, because nothing is in contact to rub.

Radiation from a pan at 250 °C is real, but it is small next to the heat that boiling moves. Latent heat does not switch off at any temperature, and a smooth level pan has no way to spin a drop.

questions.title: Roughly how hot does a smooth steel surface have to be before a water drop stops wetting it and starts to levitate on its own vapour?
questions.description: Answer in degrees Celsius, to the nearest ten, for water at ordinary atmospheric pressure.

images.alt: Two side-by-side panels show the same drop of water above the same pan surface, one labelled 150 degrees Celsius and one labelled 250 degrees Celsius. Each has flames beneath it and a question mark under the caption asking how long the drop lasts.

questions.explanation:
For water on a smooth surface, the Leidenfrost point sits near 193 °C, and most kitchen guides round it to 200 °C. It is not a constant of nature. The threshold moves with surface roughness, with the material, with dissolved contaminants, and with pressure. A textured or superhydrophobic surface can hold a vapour film well below the smooth-surface number.

There is a second, tidier definition. Plot how much heat a hot surface can hand to boiling water against how far above 100 °C that surface sits, and the curve has a minimum. The Leidenfrost point is that minimum, the coldest a surface can be and still keep a complete vapour blanket. It is therefore also the temperature at which a hovering drop lasts longest. Any hotter and radiation through the film starts carrying heat again.

questions.title: A hot plate well above the Leidenfrost point is machined with sawtooth teeth that all lean the same way. You set a levitating drop down on it. What does the drop do?

images.alt: Cross-section of a hot metal plate whose top surface is cut into sawtooth teeth that all lean the same way. A round water drop hovers above the tooth tips with short arrows showing vapour escaping beneath it. Dashed arrows point left and right from the drop, each ending in a question mark. A caption notes that the plate is level, not tilted.

options.text: It sets off in one direction along the teeth and keeps going, even slightly uphill
It stays put, because the teeth give it more surface to rest on
It wanders at random, the way it does on a smooth plate
It spins in place above the teeth without travelling along the plate

questions.explanation:
A levitating drop is held up by vapour escaping from underneath it. On a smooth plate that vapour leaves in every direction equally, so the drop coasts wherever the last nudge sent it. Sawtooth teeth break the symmetry. The vapour follows the shallow face of each tooth rather than the steep one, and the lopsided flow drags the drop with it.

The thrust is tiny. It matters only because the drag is tinier still, since the drop touches nothing, so the drop accelerates until the two balance, at a few centimetres per second. Linke and colleagues published the effect in 2006 and showed that the drops will climb a gentle slope. The same trick has since been used to steer drops through a machined maze, and it is one way to move liquid around with no moving parts.

questions.title: A pot of water with an electric heater in it is already boiling hard. You keep dialling the power up. What happens to the temperature of the heater's own surface?

images.alt: A pot of water at 100 degrees Celsius holds an immersed heater coil with bubbles rising from it. Beside the pot, an arrow marked with three steps shows the power being dialled up, and a dashed box holds a question mark labelled as the temperature of the coil's own surface.

options.text: It jumps by hundreds of degrees once vapour blankets the surface, because the film carries heat away far more slowly than bubbling water did
It stays close to 100 °C for as long as any liquid water is left in the pot
It rises smoothly, a few degrees for each extra watt, with no surprises
It falls, because more vapour means more evaporation and more cooling

questions.explanation:
Boiling moves heat remarkably well, and it gets better as the surface gets hotter, right up to a limit called the critical heat flux. Below that limit, bubbles grow, tear away, and let fresh water slam back against the metal. Above it, the bubbles merge faster than they can leave, and a continuous film of vapour wraps the surface.

That is film boiling, the same insulation that keeps a Leidenfrost drop alive, seen from the other side. Now the heater is the one trapped behind the film. A heater driven at fixed power has nowhere to put the extra energy except into its own temperature, so the surface runs away in seconds while the water stays at 100 °C. Engineers call it the boiling crisis, departure from nucleate boiling, or simply burnout.

This is why the safety case for a water-cooled reactor or a high-power electronics cold plate is written around staying below the critical heat flux rather than around the average coolant temperature. The average can look fine while one hot spot has already gone dry.
questions.references: [Wikipedia: Critical heat flux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critical_heat_flux) · [Wikipedia: Boiling, including the boiling regimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boiling)

questions.title: A cosmonaut spins a T-shaped handle about its intermediate axis and lets it float free. What does the handle do next?
questions.description: The intermediate axis is the one whose moment of inertia falls between the largest and the smallest. Treat the handle as perfectly rigid.

images.alt: Two panels. Left: a T-shaped handle with three dashed principal axes through it, the horizontal one labelled intermediate, the vertical one along the stem labelled smallest, and an oblique one labelled largest. A caption notes that the largest-inertia axis points out of the page, and a curved arrow shows the handle being spun about the intermediate axis. Right: a large question mark captioned a few seconds later, with a note that nothing touches the handle again.

options.text: It flips right over, flips back, and keeps flipping at a steady interval
It keeps spinning about the axis it was given, since nothing is there to disturb it
It drifts into a spin about its long stem and stays there
It wobbles briefly, then settles into a slow tumble that never repeats

questions.explanation:
This is the Dzhanibekov effect, named for the cosmonaut Vladimir Dzhanibekov, who noticed it in 1985 when a wing nut he had spun off a bolt kept flipping as it drifted away. The mechanics were old news even then. Poinsot described the behaviour in 1834, and it sits in Goldstein's Classical Mechanics under the name intermediate axis theorem. Anyone who has thrown a tennis racket has met it as the tennis racket theorem.

A rigid body with three different moments of inertia has one axis it cannot spin cleanly about. Set it going there and the unavoidable error in the initial spin grows instead of staying small. The handle rolls a full half turn about a different axis, and then the whole process runs in reverse. Nothing acts on the handle from outside and nothing is winding down, so the flipping repeats for as long as you care to watch, with a period fixed by the initial spin and the three moments of inertia.

questions.title: Which free spins of a rigid body with three different moments of inertia hold their orientation?
questions.description: Select every spin that stays put. Assume no air, no contact, and a perfectly rigid body.

images.alt: Two panels. Left: a T-shaped handle with three dashed principal axes through it, the horizontal one labelled intermediate, the vertical one along the stem labelled smallest, and an oblique one labelled largest. A caption notes that the largest-inertia axis points out of the page, and a curved arrow shows the handle being spun about the intermediate axis. Right: a large question mark captioned a few seconds later, with a note that nothing touches the handle again.

options.text: A spin about the axis with the largest moment of inertia
A spin about the axis with the smallest moment of inertia
A spin about the intermediate axis
A spin about any axis at all, once there is nothing left to disturb it

questions.explanation:
Euler's equations for a torque-free body settle it. Disturb a spin about the largest or the smallest axis and the error stays an error. The two off-axis components trade back and forth, so the spin axis traces a small circle and goes no further. Disturb a spin about the intermediate axis and the same algebra gives exponential growth instead of oscillation, because the two coefficients that govern the wobble now share a sign instead of opposing each other. Every real spin carries some error, so in practice the intermediate axis always loses it.

The energy picture says the same thing without the algebra. At a fixed angular momentum, a spin about the largest axis is the least kinetic energy the body can have, and a spin about the smallest axis is the most. Extremes are hard to leave when both energy and momentum are fixed. The intermediate axis is neither, and a saddle point is exactly where a small push takes you somewhere else.

questions.title: While the handle flips over and back, nothing touches it. Which of these stay constant?
questions.description: Select every quantity that does not change. The handle is rigid and free.

images.alt: Two panels. Left: a T-shaped handle with three dashed principal axes through it, the horizontal one labelled intermediate, the vertical one along the stem labelled smallest, and an oblique one labelled largest. A caption notes that the largest-inertia axis points out of the page, and a curved arrow shows the handle being spun about the intermediate axis. Right: a large question mark captioned a few seconds later, with a note that nothing touches the handle again.

options.text: The angular momentum vector, in both size and direction
The rotational kinetic energy
The angular velocity vector
The angle between the handle's stem and the angular momentum vector

questions.explanation:
No external torque means the angular momentum vector is pinned in space, in size and in direction. A rigid body with nothing to dissipate energy keeps its rotational kinetic energy too. Everything you can see moving is the handle rearranging itself around those two fixed facts.

Angular velocity is not one of them. It swings around inside the body and sweeps a cone in space, and that motion is the flip. The angle between the stem and the angular momentum vector cannot hold still either, since after a flip the stem points the other way while the angular momentum has not budged.

The flip costs no energy and needs no torque, because it rearranges the same angular momentum rather than changing it. Poinsot turned this into a picture. Plot the angular velocity in body coordinates, and conservation of energy confines it to an ellipsoid while conservation of momentum confines it to a sphere, so the motion follows the curve where the two surfaces meet. Around the largest and smallest axes those curves are small closed loops. At the intermediate axis the two surfaces cross, and the curve through the crossing leads away around the body instead of closing up.

questions.title: You toss a phone three ways: a flat spin about the axis out of the screen, a roll about the axis down its long edges, and an end-over-end flip about the axis across its short edges. Which toss lands with the screen facing the other way?
questions.description: Assume a clean toss and one full rotation before it lands. The diagram marks the three axes.

images.alt: Three panels showing the same phone with a different spin axis marked in each: a flat spin about the axis straight out of the screen, a roll about the axis running down the long edges, and an end-over-end flip about the axis running across the short edges. Each panel shows a curved arrow around its axis.

options.text: The end-over-end flip
The flat spin
The long-axis roll
None of them: the extra twist comes from air resistance, so a clean toss keeps its face

questions.explanation:
Work out the three moments of inertia for a flat slab of length L and width W. About the axis out of the screen it goes with L squared plus W squared, the largest of the three. About the axis down the long edges it goes with W squared alone, the smallest. About the axis across the short edges it goes with L squared, which lands in between. The end-over-end flip is therefore a spin about the intermediate axis, the one axis that cannot keep its orientation. The phone picks up a half turn about its long axis while it flips, and arrives with the other face up.

A tennis racket does the same thing, which is where the tennis racket theorem gets its name. Hold the face horizontal, throw the racket so it turns once about the axis perpendicular to the handle, catch the handle, and the other face is up. Try the same throw about the handle axis and it stays put.

Air resistance has nothing to do with it. The half twist is a property of torque-free rotation and shows up just as readily in orbit as over a bed, which is where you should run the experiment with your own phone.

questions.title: Explorer 1 launched in 1958 spinning at 750 rpm about its long axis, the axis with the smallest moment of inertia. It was soon tumbling instead. What went wrong?

images.alt: Two panels. Left: a long, thin satellite with a nose cone and four flexible whip antennas trailing from its body, a dashed line along its length, and a curved arrow labelled 750 rpm about the long axis, its smallest moment of inertia. Right: a large question mark captioned a few hours later, noting that the spin is no longer about the axis it was given.

options.text: Its flexible whip antennas flexed and drained rotational energy, and a body that loses energy at fixed angular momentum ends up spinning about its axis of largest moment of inertia
A spin about the axis of smallest moment of inertia is unstable, so the design was never going to hold
Aerodynamic drag at orbital altitude produced a torque that tipped the satellite over
Earth's magnetic field pulled on the satellite's magnetised steel skin

questions.explanation:
For a perfectly rigid body, a spin about the smallest axis is stable, so the textbook of the day said the design was fine. Explorer 1 was not rigid. Its four whip antennas bent back and forth as it spun, and flexing metal turns rotational energy into heat.

Angular momentum had nowhere to go. Hold angular momentum fixed and bleed energy away, and the body slides toward whichever spin state carries the least kinetic energy for that momentum, which is a spin about the axis of largest moment of inertia. For a long thin satellite that means a flat tumble rather than a spin about its length, and that is what the telemetry showed.

The fix is now standard practice, the major axis rule. A passively spin-stabilised spacecraft that cannot avoid internal damping should be spun about its axis of maximum inertia. Explorer 1 found the Van Allen belts, and it also forced the first serious extension of Euler's rigid-body theory in nearly two centuries, to cover bodies that dissipate energy while conserving momentum.

questions.title: Three frictionless tracks join the same two points, A above and B lower and off to one side. Identical balls start from rest on all three at the same instant. Which one reaches B first?
questions.description: The diagram names the three tracks. All three start at A and end at B.

images.alt: Three tracks run from a point A at the upper left to a point B at the lower right: a straight ramp, a track that starts steep and then flattens out, and a track that stays shallow and then plunges. A ball sits at A, a legend names the three tracks, and a question mark beside B asks which ball arrives first.

options.text: The ball on the track that drops steeply first and then flattens out
The ball on the straight ramp, because that is the shortest path between the points
The ball on the track that stays shallow first and then plunges
They arrive together, because all three balls fall through the same height

questions.explanation:
The straight ramp is the shortest path and it loses. The winner is the track that spends its length where the ball is already fast. Drop steeply at the start and the ball is moving quickly for almost the whole journey, covering the extra distance at a speed the straight ramp does not reach until the very end.

The tie is the tempting wrong answer. Energy conservation does fix the speed at every height, identically on all three tracks, so all three balls do cross B at exactly the same speed. Speed at a point and time along a path are different questions.

Johann Bernoulli put this to the mathematicians of Europe in 1696. The answer turns out to be one particular curve, and every other steep-then-flat shape loses to it.

questions.title: The winning track is longer than the straight ramp. Why does the extra distance not cost it the race?

images.alt: Three tracks run from a point A at the upper left to a point B at the lower right: a straight ramp, a track that starts steep and then flattens out, and a track that stays shallow and then plunges. A ball sits at A, a legend names the three tracks, and a question mark beside B asks which ball arrives first.

options.text: The steep start turns height into speed early, so the ball covers most of the path faster than the ball on the straight ramp ever manages
The curve is shorter than the straight ramp once you measure only the horizontal distance covered
A curved track presses less hard on the ball, so less energy goes into friction
The ball rolls instead of sliding, so its spin carries extra energy along the curve

questions.explanation:
Travel time is distance divided by speed, added up along the path, and speed comes only from height already given up. A ball that is already low is already fast. So the quickest shape spends its height early, buys speed with it, and then uses that speed over the distance that remains.

Push the idea too far and it backfires, which is why the answer is one definite curve. Fall vertically at the start and you burn height without making progress toward B. Hug the straight line and you never get the early speed. Bernoulli found the balance with an analogy to light, treating the ball as a ray refracting through layer after layer of increasing speed, so that Snell's law at every depth traces out the curve.

All three tracks cover the same horizontal distance, since they share both endpoints, so the curve is longer by every measure. Friction is not in the problem at all. And rolling takes energy out of forward motion rather than adding any, which is why a rolling ball reaches the bottom of a ramp slower than a sliding one.

questions.title: What is the name of the curve that solves this problem, the one traced by a point on the rim of a wheel rolling along a straight line?

images.alt: Three tracks run from a point A at the upper left to a point B at the lower right: a straight ramp, a track that starts steep and then flattens out, and a track that stays shallow and then plunges. A ball sits at A, a legend names the three tracks, and a question mark beside B asks which ball arrives first.

questions.explanation:
The quickest descent is an arc of a cycloid, turned upside down so that its cusp sits at the release point. Bernoulli set the problem in June 1696 and five solutions came back: from his brother Jakob, from Leibniz, from l'Hôpital, from Tschirnhaus, and one sent anonymously. Bernoulli is said to have recognised the anonymous one at a glance, remarking that he knew the lion by its claw mark. It was Newton's, worked out the night the challenge reached him.

The same curve answers a question Christiaan Huygens had already solved in 1659 and proved geometrically in his Horologium Oscillatorium of 1673: on a cycloid, the time to slide to the bottom does not depend on where you start. Jakob Bernoulli then tried to outdo his brother with a harder version of the problem, and that led Euler to the calculus of variations. Seventeenth-century mathematicians quarrelled over the cycloid often enough that it picked up a nickname, the Helen of Geometers.

questions.title: You release two beads from rest at different heights on the same cycloid trough. Which one reaches the bottom first?

images.alt: A single U-shaped cycloid trough with two beads resting on its left flank, one higher and one lower, both marked as released from rest. A question mark below the lowest point of the trough asks which bead reaches the bottom first.

options.text: They arrive together, whatever heights they start from
The bead released higher up, because it builds more speed on the way down
The bead released lower down, because it has less distance to cover
Whichever bead is heavier

questions.explanation:
A cycloid is a tautochrone, from the Greek for equal time. Release a bead anywhere on it and the slide to the bottom takes the same time. The higher bead has further to travel and it travels faster, and on this particular curve those two effects cancel exactly, at every starting height.

On a cycloid the restoring force along the track is proportional to the distance along the track from the bottom, which is the definition of simple harmonic motion, and a harmonic oscillator's period does not depend on its amplitude. A pendulum swinging along a cycloid therefore keeps time at any swing, unlike one swinging along a circular arc, which runs slow as it swings wider.

Huygens saw the application immediately. Bend a pendulum's path into a cycloid and the clock keeps the same time however hard it is pushed. Clockmakers took the other road. Hooke's anchor escapement cut the swing to a few degrees, where a circular arc is close enough to a cycloid that the difference stopped mattering.

questions.title: Now B sits far off to the side. The sideways distance from A is three times the drop from A down to B. Where does the fastest frictionless track go?

images.alt: Point A at the upper left and point B at the lower right, joined by a dashed straight line marked as a reference only. Dimension arrows show that the sideways distance from A to B is three times the drop h from A down to B. A caption asks which frictionless track from A to B is quickest, followed by a question mark.

options.text: It dives below the level of B and then climbs back up to reach it
Straight from A to B, since a drop that small is not worth a detour
Along the same shape as before, staying above the straight line the whole way
Vertically down from A, then flat along the level of B

questions.explanation:
A cycloid arc that starts from a cusp at A reaches its lowest point after travelling sideways about 1.57 times the distance it has fallen, since that ratio is pi over two. Put the target further out than that and the curve has to pass its own bottom and climb back, so the quickest route dips below the finish before rising to it. At a sideways distance of three drops, it is well past that point.

Going below B is not wasted motion. The deep stretch is where the ball is fastest, and the time saved crossing it more than pays for the climb at the end. The limiting case makes this plain. When B sits at exactly the same height as A, the answer is a full turn of the cycloid, down and back up again, and it still beats the flat track, along which the ball would never move at all.
